title: Baruch atah
hook: read the opening words of every blessing

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shema Yisrael: two words, a silent eye, a dot that moved to the left. Your line was read it yourself. Did you say them before sleep? Today, two more words, the ones that open a blessing. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-five.

Friday evening, a kitchen. Two candles are lit, and before anyone eats, someone lifts a cup of wine and starts to speak. Then a hand rests on the bread, and someone speaks again. A new fruit in season, a glass of water, thunder outside, new clothes put on for the first time: in the prayer book there's a blessing for each, and the formula opens the same way. Two words come first, over and over, like the first two notes of a song the whole family knows. Baruch atah. If you learned to read them, you'd see them at the top of page after page.
screen: `CANDLES, WINE, BREAD.` → `A BLESSING FOR EACH.` → `THE SAME TWO WORDS FIRST.`

segments.voice: Baruch atah. Turn it four ways. First, baruch. Bet, with a dot inside it, so it says b, not v, and the T-shaped mark under it: ba. Resh, then a vav with a dot in its belly, which says oo: ru. And at the end, the long-tailed final chaf, one of the five endings, a breathy ch. Ba, ruch. Baruch. Blessed. Second, atah. Alef, silent, carrying a short line under it: ah. Then tav, with a dot inside and the T-shaped mark: ta. Then heh, which here, at the end of the word, stays silent. A, tah. Atah. You. Third, who "you" is. The words are already in the Bible, in Psalm 119: "Blessed art Thou, O LORD; teach me Thy statutes." After baruch atah comes the name of God, which is not read as it is written. In prayer it's said Adonai, and outside prayer some say Hashem, the Name, instead. Then come the words for our God, king of the world. The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, records two teachers' views: a blessing without the Name is not a blessing, and a blessing without God's kingship is not a blessing. Fourth, a turn some readers notice. Baruch atah speaks straight to God: you. Then listen to the blessing over bread as it goes on: hamotzi, who brings forth bread from the earth. It has moved from speaking to God to speaking about God. Close and far in a single sentence. The blessing begins face to face.
screen: `BARUCH: BA, RUCH, BLESSED.` · `ATAH: A, TAH, YOU.` · `THEN THE NAME, AND THE KING.` · `FACE TO FACE, THEN ABOUT.` · then, large: `בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read them aloud. Settle, and breathe. Look at the screen. Start at the right. Ba, ruch. Baruch. Then a, tah. Atah. Say them aloud once, slowly, so you can hear each letter. Then a second time, a little more smoothly. Then let them go, and sit with the shape they leave: someone speaking directly, saying you. Notice one thing in front of you right now: a cup, a window, your own hands. If you pray, you can say a blessing you know over it. The bell holds the time.
Baruch atah. Blessed are you: the two words that open the blessings, read in Hebrew, right to left. Today's word.
Your line: baruch atah. Today, before you eat or drink something, pause for the length of those two words and notice what's in your hand. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Jews say blessings before eating and drinking, over Sabbath candles and wine, and at many other moments; the standard blessing opens with baruch atah, then God's name, read Adonai, and the words for king of the world.

fork.setup: a blessing opens baruch atah: blessed are you. who is the "you"?
fork.reveal: God, addressed face to face. then comes the Name, and the words for king of the world.

original.note: Hebrew: blessed are you, the opening of the standard blessing.

trapdoor: what you thought: a blessing is a wish for good things to happen to you.
what it means: a Jewish blessing opens by speaking to God directly: blessed are you.
what a scholar hears: Berakhot 40b records one teacher requiring the Name and another requiring God's kingship for a blessing to count.

sources.quoted: Blessed art Thou, O LORD; teach me Thy statutes.

notes: Psalms 119:12 quoted as JPS 1917; confirm exact wording and capitalization ('Thou', 'Thy').
Berakhot 40b paraphrased: Rabbi Yochanan's view that a blessing lacking the Name and malchut is not a blessing. Confirm the folio and fair framing as 'records the view'.
The hook's list (new fruit, thunder, new shoes) are blessing occasions in the prayer book; new clothes and thunder have blessings, though the formula after baruch atah varies. Confirm.
Shift from second to third person described as something 'some readers notice'; 'many blessings' is a description of the liturgy, not of people. Confirm or soften.
Index hook says 'every blessing'; script says 'the formula opens the same way' and 'the standard blessing' to avoid an every-claim.

Editor pass: Berakhot 40b now attributed as two views (Rav: the Name; Rabbi Yochanan: kingship) instead of one combined view; 'many blessings switch' replaced with the concrete case of the blessing over bread (hamotzi); 'new shoes' and 'a first bite of the day' replaced with new clothes and a glass of water (blessing occasions in the prayer book); fixed the garbled practice line 'speaking directly, as you'.
